author: haiku
reason: A opens with a one-paragraph summary of the whole flow (watermark, paged download into staging, catch-up, atomic swap, throttled incremental), keeps one consistent trigger/action/data/state/failure layout for every step, and closes with a table of what the rep sees in each state; B spreads its state across a status, a resync flag and generation pointers, and starts with setup steps before the actual flow.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow. It opens with a one-paragraph summary of the whole flow and says plainly which steps are the main flow and which are shared rules. It also lists each state field in one place and explains, case by case, why catch-up misses nothing. A gives the retry rule twice and spreads the resume logic across the dispatcher, step 6 and step 11. That overlap makes it harder to trace what starts each step.

author: haiku
reason: B is quicker to follow: it starts with a plain overview of the two sync modes, explains why catch-up makes the paged download correct, and uses an explicit `phase` field and a separate triggers section to show how a resume works, while A packs many state fields and edge-case reasoning into dense terms and step blocks before the reader has the big picture (though B's step numbers clash with its numbered sub-steps).

author: haiku
reason: A defines every term in plain language before using it and gives each numbered step the same short Starts/Data/Failure layout, so an engineer new to the project can follow the flow quickly; B is more thorough, but its dense edge-case reasoning, especially the open-read swap wait, slows a first read.

author: sonnet
reason: B is quicker to follow because it opens with a three-part lifecycle (build, incremental sync, resync) mapped to step numbers, each step ends with an explicit "Next" pointer, and its state is simpler (a build phase plus a stale flag), while A makes the reader track a seven-value download_status state machine through denser cross-referenced steps.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a three-part lifecycle map, routes every run from one decision step (step 3) and gives each step an explicit "Next:" link, so the flow is easier to follow than B's seven-status state machine, where some logic sits in odd places (for example, the disk-space check under "On failure", and the cellular pause split across steps 3 and 4).

author: sonnet

author: haiku
reason: A is easier to follow because of three things: a table of where each piece of state lives, a straight checklist that marks what starts each step, what it changes and what happens if it fails, and Abort and Rollback written out once as shared procedures. B's glossary is useful, but its lock-before-build ordering, its split between a pipeline run and a watch job, and its rolled_back_from and previous_release bookkeeping take more effort to piece together.
